findings.statement: CXCR2, the top convergence gene, has no literature_relation records in this corpus (zero extracted relations); its literature score comes only from the Open Targets association, and clinical-stage CXCR1 and CXCR2 antagonists (reparixin, navarixin, ladarixin, SX-682) exist in Open Targets. Corpus support for CXCR2 itself is only indirect, through its ligand CXCL8 (see CXCL8), so no corpus sentence shows that blocking CXCR2 is therapeutic in UC.

CXCL8 is reported as a driver of UC through the axis of CXCL8 with CXCR1 and CXCR2 (PI3K/Akt, MAPK, NF-kappaB), as a PPI hub gene in UC, and as a blood diagnostic marker for IBD in a validation RNA-seq cohort. Evidence is bioinformatic and review-level; the anti-IL-8 antibodies in Open Targets (ABX-IL8, adakitug) are phase 2 at most.

IDO1 is the best mechanistically supported candidate: expression is elevated in UC patients and correlates with M1 macrophage polarization, IDO1 drives M1 polarization through the ER-stress GRP78-XBP1 pathway, and a methyl-tryptophan IDO inhibitor ameliorated DSS colitis. This is a single study (PMID 40370742) in mouse plus human data, and no UC clinical trial of IDO1 inhibitors is evidenced; approved/clinical IDO1 drugs are oncology compounds.

MMP1 is reported as a diagnostic marker (strong AUC) in a bioinformatic study of UC-associated CRC, correlates with macrophage infiltration, and mirikizumab-modified transcripts including MMP1, MMP3, S100A8 and IL1B correlate with Mayo, Geboes and Robarts indices. The inhibitor ilomastat appears only as a docking prediction, so therapeutic evidence is computational.

CHI3L1 is upregulated in UC and correlates with NLRP3 inflammasome expression; it promotes macrophage pyroptosis via the BCAT1/NF-kappaB axis, and its inhibition was protective in experimental work. Velpatasvir binding to recombinant CHI3L1 was confirmed by microscale thermophoresis, a repurposing hit at micromolar affinity with no clinical data. No CHI3L1 drug is listed in Open Targets.

DUOX2 is among the most elevated proteins in inflamed UC biopsies versus healthy controls, and is named with S100A8, IL-1B, CXCL1, MMP10 and others as a credible biomarker for diagnosis and therapy. It is linked to ferroptosis and a herbal formula (TLXDS) that inhibits DUOX2; this support is single-study and preclinical, and no DUOX2 drug exists.

AQP9 is predominantly expressed in neutrophils, upregulated in mouse UC colon, and promotes NET formation through JAK2-STAT3-mediated pyroptosis, aggravating epithelial injury. Evidence is concentrated in a few recent papers using mouse models and bioinformatics, and there is no AQP9 drug.

S100A9 is overexpressed in colitis, reported to perform excellently in diagnosing active UC by ROC, and is upregulated in UC by ONT-RNA-seq. In a tofacitinib single-cell study, S100A9 was downregulated in resident macrophages in responders, which suggests the signal partly reflects myeloid cells rather than epithelium.

In a tofacitinib single-cell study, non-responders showed increased macrophage and fibroblast activation after treatment, with upregulation of MMP9, IL1B, IL6, CXCL1, CXCL8 and S100A9 versus baseline. IL1B is also listed as a candidate diagnostic biomarker. This ties the inflammatory signature to non-response to JAK inhibition, though it is a single cohort.

CXCL1 is reported as a diagnostic or activity marker in several bioinformatic studies, but individual discrimination is modest: one study reported only modest ROC discrimination for CXCL1 alone, while a combined five-gene model performed much better. CXCL1 is also overexpressed in pancolitis. No drug targets CXCL1.

LCN2 expression is higher in UC than normal tissue, but declines with disease duration and is lower in UC-associated cancer than in long-duration UC. It is proposed as a diagnostic biomarker for UC-associated carcinogenesis, so the direction relative to dysplasia is non-monotonic.

HMGCS2 is downregulated in UC (with AQP8) and described as having high diagnostic value, supporting the epithelial metabolic-loss signature; evidence is bioinformatic with limited experimental validation.

CD274 (PD-L1) ranks high on expression and Open Targets, with approved checkpoint antibodies for oncology, but has no literature_relation records in this corpus. Bioinformatic papers name CD274 with MMP1, NCF2 and PLAU as hub genes associated with macrophage infiltration in UC; there is no evidence in the retrieved sentences that PD-L1 blockade or agonism is therapeutic in UC.

OSMR and JAK2 have strong Open Targets association and tractability (vixarelimab phase 2 for OSMR; JAK inhibitors for JAK2), but no literature_relation records here. Oncostatin M appears only as a predicted upstream regulator in pathway analysis, and the corpus contains no sentence directly linking OSM/OSMR to anti-TNF non-response.

caveats: Many top-ranked genes (CXCR2, CXCR1, CD274, FCGR2A, JAK2, IL2RA, OSMR, PI3, DUOXA2, CXCL5, REG1A, CDH3) have zero extracted literature relations; their literature score reflects Open Targets only.
Most literature support is bioinformatic hub-gene or ROC analysis with few experimental validations; the corpus is about 300 abstracts and is not a systematic review.
Numeric values from sentences (AUCs) were not bound to record fields and are described in words.
Immune-cell origin (neutrophil, macrophage) of S100A9, AQP9, IL1B and CXCL8 signals means bulk expression may not indicate epithelial change.
Genes not examined in detail: MMP3, MMP7, MMP9, MMP10, SERPINB5, SLC26A2, CCL2, NOS2, S100A8, REG3A, and others.
